name: Ash rose
lede: Ash rose is a dusty, greyed pink-brown that sits in the same small family as Old Rose and Dusty Puce, and that our own library files alongside a Japanese traditional name that translates, almost too fittingly, as "cherry blossom mouse grey."

sections.title: A rose with the color taken out of it
sections.body: The name follows a pattern common to the whole dusty-rose family: take a flower name, rose, and grey it down with a second word that signals the muting, here "ash" [1]. The real 1955 ISCC-NBS filing for the exact name Ash Rose lands on block 19, "grayish red" [2]; our own graph's computed-nearest block for this hex lands one neighborhood over, block 18, "light grayish red," only 3.1 units off [1]. Our library also files an identical or near-identical color under Dusty Puce, a separate cross-system name for roughly the same dusty pink-brown [1]. Most strikingly, it sits beside Sakuranezumi (桜鼠), a traditional Japanese name that translates as "cherry blossom mouse grey" — two unrelated naming traditions, a Western flower-plus-modifier name and a Japanese animal-plus-flower name, landing on nearly the same muted pink [1]. Neither explains the other; it is coincidence in color space, not shared history.

sections.title: A crowded family of dusty pinks
sections.body: In the color graph, Ash Rose sits 4.4 units from [[antique-rose]], more vivid, and 4.5 from [[marie-antoinette]], almost the same color [3]. [[rosy-brown]], 4.8 off, is lighter; [[old-rose]], 5.2 off, is more vivid again; [[mauve-rose]], 5.8 off, is redder; [[brownish-vinaceous]], 5.9 off, is lighter and redder [3]. That is six separate named colors within six units of each other, all variations on the same basic idea of a greyed, dusty pink-brown — the dusty-rose family is one of the most crowded small neighborhoods in the whole graph.

sections.title: Seen in
sections.body: Among design aesthetics, the closest full-palette match is Angelcore, 3.4 units off on this exact swatch, with Millennial pink a step further at 4.8 units on its neighbor Old Rose, and Decora at 5.5 on Rosy Brown [4]. Three garments in our own archive land close by, and they span three continents and a very wide span of time: a Paracas turban band from Peru's South Coast, 1.4 units off; an early-twentieth-century cover from Sri Lanka, 1.9 off; and a length of copperplate-printed cotton from France, 2.3 off [5]. Its nearest gem twin is the broad diamond and colored-diamond family, 9.3 units off, more a loose family resemblance than a close match [6].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this color in 84 of 23,778 paintings, about 0.35 percent as photographed; a stricter within-painting lens finds it in 39 [7]. That makes it rarer than 55 percent of the named colors in the archive [7]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, 51 percent of its 39 clearest matches, the least visible rank by lightness within the canvas, by far its most common role [7]. It is sharply over-represented in paintings from India, 2.5 times the expected rate across 721 paintings, and in the Pahari school of Indian miniature painting specifically, 4.2 times expected across 118 works [7]. Named painters carrying it here include Mary Cassatt, Henri Matisse, Henri-Edmond Cross and Georges Lacombe, though none individually stands out as sharply as the India and Pahari numbers do [7].

It peaks century-wide in the 1900s, 0.4 percent of 1,674 paintings from then, 2.2 times expected, and the single-decade peak is a touch earlier, the 1890s, at the same 2.2 times lift [7]. The earliest match in the archive is from the year 1000, with 54 dated paintings carrying it through to 1922; the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first [7]. In printed English, the word "rose" in all its senses, the flower, the name, the color, and the color name together, peaks in the 2010s and rose fastest in the 1980s, which tells us more about the word than about this specific dusty pink [7]. This is a computed color match on photographed, varnished canvases, not a pigment test.

origin.named_after: a descriptive compound: "rose" muted by "ash"; the exact coinage is undocumented in the sources consulted

openers: A Japanese traditional name for almost this same dusty pink translates as "cherry blossom mouse grey."
Ash Rose is one of six closely related dusty-pink names crowded into the same small patch of color space.

issues: Depth wave pilot: no book concordance or 1930/1912 dictionary entry exists for this name, so depth comes entirely from measured data: the color graph's real look-alikes and traditional-name cross-reference, archive fieldnotes, and garment/gem/look twins. States plainly that the exact coinage is undocumented.
